  s <- formatC(abs(x), format = "f", digits = d, big.mark = ",")
  ifelse(x < 0, paste0("−", s), s)
}

## Introduction

::: {.report-intro}
![](assets/opa/opa-details.png){.opa-figure}

This report rebuilds, step by step, RJKDC's fiscal estimate of California's
Proposition 40 (the Billionaire Tax Act): a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of billionaires
resident in California on 1 January 2026. The authors argue that the tax would collect far less
than the [BSZ report](../../bsz-analysis/site/) estimates, and that billionaires who leave take their income tax with them for
ever, so the state ends up poorer. Following the
[Open Policy Analysis](https://doi.org/10.1093/scipol/scaa067) framework:

- **Open Output**: [the explorer](explorer/), the mean net present value and share of
  negative outcomes for every combination of seven inputs
- **Open Analysis**: this document, and [the slide deck](slides/slides.html)
- **Open Materials**: [the repository](https://github.com/fhoces/opa-prop40/tree/main/rjkdc-analysis), every script, test, CSV and
  source (guide, with all nine mismatches found along the way: [the materials page](materials.html))
:::

**What is reproduced.** Jaros and Rauh, *The Net Present Value of the California Billionaire Tax Act*,
NBER chapter c15504 (22 September 2026; NBER is the National Bureau of Economic Research, which
circulates working papers), the litigation-weighted revision of the first version by Rauh, Jaros,
Kearney, Doran and Cosso (SSRN 6340778, March 2026; SSRN is a preprint site). Its headline:
revenue of about \$30B (\$`r h("nber","revenue_range_low","printed")`B to
\$`r h("nber","revenue_range_high","printed")`B) and a mean NPV of
`r num(h("nber","mc_mean_npv","printed"))` \$B, with `r h("nber","mc_pct_negative","printed")`%
of simulated outcomes negative (the Figure 3 note, PDF p.35; the text on p.1 says 85%). That mean
NPV is **the main estimate**, derived step by
step in [the next section](#the-main-estimate).^[The authors released a first version in March
2026: Rauh, Jaros, Kearney, Doran and Cosso, Hoover Institution, SSRN 6340778. It printed revenue
of about \$`r h("ssrn","revenue_headline","printed")`B and a mean NPV of
`r num(h("ssrn","mc_mean_npv","printed"))` \$B, with `r h("ssrn","mc_pct_negative","printed")`%
of outcomes negative (its PDF p.1). The pipeline reproduces it too; the
[appendix](#appendix-first-version) at the end of this report sets out what it printed and
which checks concern it.]

The analysis is reproduced from the authors' own public, MIT-licensed code and data
([github.com/bjaros20/wealth_tax](https://github.com/bjaros20/wealth_tax), pinned at commit
`25e84dd`): their Excel workbook is read cell by cell, their R scripts are ported line by line
and also re-run unmodified, and the person-level file `final.csv` is summed directly. Every
number in this document is read from the project's `{targets}` pipeline at render time; the only
numbers typed in are the paper's printed values we compare against, each with its PDF page
(page numbers are PDF pages throughout).

**The shape of the argument**, in one line: net present value = wealth tax collected once, minus
the present value of the income tax that departing billionaires would have paid in every future
year. Sections 4 and 5.1 of the paper estimate the two pieces; Sections 5.2 to 5.4 combine them.
We follow that order.

### Notation, in one place

| Symbol | Meaning | Unit |
|---|---|---|
| $\tau$ | statutory wealth tax rate | share |
| $WT$ | one-time wealth tax revenue actually collected | \$B |
| $C$ | annual California income tax paid by the billionaires | \$B per year |
| $f$ | share of that income tax base that leaves the state | share |
| $r$ | real discount rate (the Monte Carlo's draw) | per year |
| $g$ | real growth of the lost income tax stream | per year |
| $\varepsilon$ | migration semi-elasticity: % of the base lost per percentage point of tax | |
| $q$ | probability the Act survives constitutional challenge | probability |
| NPV | $WT - f \cdot C/r$ (or $/(r-g)$), the net fiscal effect today | \$B |

## The main estimate, step by step {#the-main-estimate}

The main estimate is the paper's mean net present value, printed as
**`r num(h("nber","mc_mean_npv","printed"))` \$B** (PDF p.1 and p.35). The authors get it from a
Monte Carlo: they draw four inputs at random 100,000 times, compute
$NPV = WT - f \cdot C / r$ for each draw, and average. Because the four draws are independent,
the average has an exact value too, and we build it one input at a time. Every number below is
read from the pipeline (`R/npv_mc.R`, `R/nber_final.R`); the draw ranges are the defaults of
`compute_npv_mc_nber()`, which copies the authors' script `NPV_dist_v8.R`.

### Step 1: the wealth tax collected, $WT$

The script draws $WT \sim U[`r nb$wt_min`, `r nb$wt_max`]$ (\$B). The top, `r nb$wt_max`, is
the revenue if the Act survives in court, after removing the seven confirmed departures. Summing
the authors' person-level file `final.csv` gives \$`r num(nc$ceiling_recomputed, 2)`B for the same
quantity, so the script's round 72 is close ([mismatch 4](materials.html#mismatches)). The bottom,
`r nb$wt_min`, is the Act struck down. The mean of the draw is
$$E[WT] = \frac{`r nb$wt_min` + `r nb$wt_max`}{2} = `r num((nb$wt_min + nb$wt_max) / 2, 2)`.$$
This is the paper's central revenue, $q \times 72$ with a survival chance $q$ = 0.50
(PDF p.33). The 0 lower bound is **guesswork**.

### Step 2: the share of the income tax base that leaves, $f$

The script draws $f \sim U[`r nb$f_min`, `r nb$f_max`]$, on its own, unrelated to the revenue
draw. Its mean is $E[f]$ = `r num((nb$f_min + nb$f_max) / 2, 2)`: on average, 45 cents of every
dollar of billionaire income tax leaves the state. The range is **guesswork**, "centered
conservatively around the observed wealth-base departure fraction" (PDF p.31).

### Step 3: the income tax the billionaires pay each year, $C$

The script draws $C \sim U[`r nb$c_min`, `r nb$c_max`]$ (\$B a year), the two ends of the income
tax Monte Carlo in [Section 5.1](#section-5.1-the-income-tax-the-billionaires-pay). Its mean is
$E[C]$ = `r num((nb$c_min + nb$c_max) / 2, 2)`.

### Step 4: the discount rate, $r$

The script draws $r \sim U[`r nb$rg_min`, `r nb$rg_max`]$, a rate between
`r pct(100 * nb$rg_min)` and `r pct(100 * nb$rg_max)` a year. A stream of
\$1 a year for ever is worth $1/r$ today, so what enters is the mean of $1/r$, not $1/E[r]$:
$$E\!\left[\tfrac1r\right] = \frac{\ln(`r nb$rg_max` / `r nb$rg_min`)}{`r nb$rg_max` - `r nb$rg_min`} = `r num(npv_e_inv_rate(nb$rg_min, nb$rg_max), 2)`.$$
In words: at these rates, \$1 lost every year for ever is worth about
\$`r num(npv_e_inv_rate(nb$rg_min, nb$rg_max), 0)` today. The range is **guesswork**: its
`r pct(100 * nb$rg_min)` anchor is a published market yield, which is why the export contract (the
two CSV files, `inputs.csv` and `outputs.csv`, that each analysis's pipeline writes for the
comparison to read) and the comparison's
[disputes row 2](https://github.com/fhoces/opa-prop40/blob/main/comparison/DISPUTES.md) call the
range research, but the width of the band, to `r pct(100 * nb$rg_max)`, is the authors' judgement,
and the width is what moves the result.

### Step 5: the present value of the income tax lost

The three loss inputs are independent, so the mean of their product is the product of their means:
$$E\!\left[\frac{f\,C}{r}\right] = `r num((nb$f_min + nb$f_max) / 2, 2)` \times `r num((nb$c_min + nb$c_max) / 2, 2)` \times `r num(npv_e_inv_rate(nb$rg_min, nb$rg_max), 2)` = `r num(h("nber","pv_lost"), 2)`.$$

### Step 6: the net present value

The revenue of Step 1 minus the loss of Step 5:
$$E[NPV] = E[WT] - E\!\left[\frac{f\,C}{r}\right]$$
$$= `r num(h("nber","mc_expected_revenue"), 2)` - `r num(h("nber","pv_lost"), 2)` = `r num(tr("npv_mc_nber_analytic_mean"), 2)`.$$

The authors do not print this exact expectation (the average of the Monte Carlo computed by
formula rather than by drawing). They print the average of one seeded run of 100,000 draws (a
seeded run: one run of the random draws started from a fixed seed number, 2026, so it gives the
same draws every time; its mean differs from the exact expectation by sampling error), which our
R port replays draw for draw:
**`r num(mcn$summary$mean, 3)` \$B**, printed as `r num(h("nber","mc_mean_npv","printed"))`.
The two differ by `r num(abs(mcn$summary$mean - tr("npv_mc_nber_analytic_mean")), 2)` \$B, less
than one Monte Carlo standard error (`r num(mcn$summary$sd, 1)` / $\sqrt{100{,}000}$ =
`r num(mcn$summary$sd / sqrt(mcn$summary$n), 2)`). The overview and the explorer show the printed
`r num(h("nber","mc_mean_npv","printed"))`; the explorer's grid holds the exact value for every other
setting. The [explorer](explorer/) moves each of the four draws, and two readings the code does
not implement (a litigation multiplier and growth of the lost income).

```{r}
#| label: main-estimate-code
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
# The code behind this section, read from R/ and py/ at render time so it cannot drift.
grab <- function(path, start_pat) {
  l <- readLines(path, warn = FALSE); i <- grep(start_pat, l)[1]
  # R: up to the closing brace in column 1; Python: up to the next unindented line
  nxt <- if (grepl("[.]R$", path)) which(seq_along(l) > i & l == "}") + 1
         else which(seq_along(l) > i & grepl("^[^[:space:]#]", l))
  j <- if (length(nxt)) nxt[1] - 1 else length(l)
  while (j > i && !nzchar(trimws(l[j]))) j <- j - 1
  l[i:j]
}
fold <- function(summary, lang, code) {
  cat('\n<details class="code-fold"><summary>', summary, '</summary>\n\n```', lang, '\n',
      paste(code, collapse = "\n"), '\n```\n\n</details>\n\n', sep = "")
}
fold("R code for the main estimate", "r", c(
  "# R/npv_mc.R: the seeded Monte Carlo (the printed number) and the exact expectation.",
  grab("../R/npv_mc.R", "^compute_npv_mc_nber <- function"), "",
  grab("../R/npv_mc.R", "^npv_mc_summary <- function"), "",
  grab("../R/npv_mc.R", "^npv_e_inv_rate <- function"), "",
  grab("../R/npv_mc.R", "^npv_expectation <- function"), "",
  "# _targets.R: the targets this section reads",
  grep("npv_mc_nber|nber_ceiling", readLines("../_targets.R"), value = TRUE)))
fold("Python code for the main estimate", "python", c(
  "# py/npv_mc.py: the Python twin. numpy's random stream differs from R's, so its seeded",
  "# mean agrees with R's within Monte Carlo error; the exact expectation agrees exactly.",
  grab("../py/npv_mc.py", "^def compute_npv_mc_nber"), "",
  grab("../py/npv_mc.py", "^def npv_mc_summary"), "",
  grab("../py/npv_mc.py", "^def npv_mc_analytic_mean")))
```

## Section 4: the wealth tax revenue

### 4.1 The baseline, before anyone leaves (eqs. 1 and 2)

$$R_{\text{base}} = \sum_{i=1}^{N} \tau \times \text{TaxBase}_i, \qquad \text{TaxBase}_i = \text{NetWorth}_i - \text{TRRE}_i$$

In words: take each of the $N$ = `r inp("n_billionaires")` California billionaires on the 2025
Forbes list (with the authors' corrections), subtract their directly held residential real estate
(TRRE, total residential real estate; the Act exempts it), multiply what is left by the
`r pct(100*inp("tax_rate"),0)` rate, and add up. Their aggregate net worth is
\$`r num(inp("baseline_net_worth"))`B. The authors' workbook sums this row by row to
**\$`r num(rc$baseline_precise, 2)`B**; the paper prints \$`r num(out("revenue_baseline","printed_value"), 2)`B
(PDF p.19, eq. 2). The difference is [mismatch 6](materials.html#mismatches).

The tax is assessed on net worth at 31 December 2026, so the authors grow every net worth by
`r pct(100 * inp("nber_growth_rate"), 0)` to that valuation date and rebuild the base person by
person in `final.csv`: `r nc$n_domestic` domestic rows, face value
**\$`r num(nc$domestic_total_grown, 2)`B** (printed \$`r out("nber_domestic_grown","printed_value")`B,
PDF p.19). That is exactly `r num(nc$domestic_total_grown / rc$baseline_precise, 4)` times the
workbook's \$`r num(rc$baseline_precise, 2)`B, so the person-level file and the workbook agree with
each other, and both differ from the printed \$`r num(out("revenue_baseline","printed_value"), 2)`B. The
`r nc$n_international` non-US-citizen residents (\$`r num(nc$international_net_worth, 1)`B of net
worth) stay outside the base (PDF p.17).

### 4.2 The collectibility principle (eq. 3)

$$E[R] = q \times R_{\text{recognized}}$$

The authors count revenue only when it is "more likely than not" to be collected. They borrow this
test from the accounting rule for uncertain tax positions in company accounts (ASC 740-10,
PDF p.20). It works at two levels. For each taxpayer: confirmed departures, pre-filing departures
and billionaires imputed from a Pareto curve are left out of the recognized base,
$R_{\text{recognized}}$. For the Act as a whole: $q$ is the probability that the Act survives
constitutional challenge, set at `r num(ncol$q, 2)` (PDF pp.19-20). That value comes from the accounting
standard's 50% threshold, not from a legal assessment of the challenges, so it is **guesswork**.

### 4.3 The seven confirmed departures (Table 7, eq. 4)

Page, Brin, Thiel, Hankey, Spielberg, Kalanick and Sacks moved out between the initiative's filing
and the 1 January 2026 residency date (Table 7, PDF p.21). Removing their
\$`r num(nc$removed_departed_total, 2)`B leaves **\$`r num(nc$ceiling_recomputed, 2)`B** in
`final.csv`. The paper (eq. 4, p.22) and the authors' README print
\$`r out("nber_ceiling","printed_value")`B, the difference of two figures each rounded to two
decimals (`r num(nc$domestic_total_grown, 2)` − `r num(nc$removed_departed_total, 2)`), and the
script hard-codes `r nb$wt_max` ([mismatch 4](materials.html#mismatches)): one unrounded value,
its rounding and a round literal. The paper then asks how big a behavioural response that is.
It divides the share of revenue lost by the rate change, in percentage points (eq. 4, PDF p.22):

$$\varepsilon = \frac{\%\Delta \text{TaxBase}}{\Delta \text{TaxRate (p.p.)}}
 = \frac{(100.9 - 72.06)/100.9}{5}$$

```{r}
#| label: semi-elasticity
#| code-summary: "R code for the implied semi-elasticity"
eps7 <- 100 * (1 - nc$ceiling_recomputed / nc$domestic_total_grown) / (100 * inp("tax_rate"))
eps7
```

This gives `r num(eps7, 2)` (printed 5.73): a 1-point tax rate rise drives out about
`r num(eps7, 1)`% of the base. The authors treat this as a floor, because it counts only
departures that made the news (PDF pp.22-24).

### 4.4 The litigation discount and the collectible estimate (eqs. 5 to 8)

Removing three pre-filing departures as well (\$`r num(ncol$removed_prefiling, 2)`B) leaves
\$`r num(ncol$collectible_base, 2)`B (printed \$71.17B, PDF p.22). Mark Zuckerberg announced his
move in February 2026, after the residency date. The authors exclude his
\$`r num(ncol$zuckerberg, 2)`B, because collecting it depends on the retroactive date surviving in
court. That leaves a recognized base of **\$`r num(ncol$recognized, 2)`B** (eq. 5). Multiplying by
$q$ = `r num(ncol$q, 2)` gives

$$E[R] = q \times R_{\text{recognized}} = `r num(ncol$q, 2)` \times `r num(ncol$recognized, 2)` = `r num(ncol$central, 2)`$$

(printed \$`r h("nber","revenue_headline","printed")`B, eqs. 6 and 8, PDF p.23). Keeping
Zuckerberg gives \$`r num(ncol$upper, 2)`B (eq. 7). Moving the gray-zone names out gives
\$`r num(ncol$lower, 2)`B: these are the seven billionaires with departure signals short of
confirmation, plus Jan Koum, Reed Hastings and Andy Fang, reported as considering a move
(PDF p.23). Hence the printed range, \$`r h("nber","revenue_range_low","printed")`B to
\$`r h("nber","revenue_range_high","printed")`B, around "approximately \$30 billion".

The Monte Carlo does not use this point estimate. It draws revenue from 0 to 72, whose mean is the
paper's central \$`r num(h("nber","mc_expected_revenue"), 0)`B (Step 1 and
[Section 5.4](#monte-carlo)).

### 4.5 Validation against the literature (Table 8)

$$\eta_{\text{mig}} = 0.24 \times 43 = 10.32, \qquad \text{base lost} = 1 - (1 - 0.05)^{10.32}$$

```{r}
#| label: log-form
#| code-summary: "R code for the literature-implied base loss"
lit_loss <- 1 - (1 - inp("tax_rate"))^inp("brulhart_semi_elasticity")
lit_loss
```

Brülhart et al. (2022) estimate that Swiss taxable wealth falls by about 43% per point of wealth
tax, about 24% of it through people moving. The authors keep only the moving part,
`r inp("brulhart_semi_elasticity")`, and apply it to the 5-point rate in log form: the base
shrinks by **`r pct(100 * lit_loss)`** (PDF p.24). Table 8 (PDF p.25) sets this beside the observed
28.6% from the seven confirmed departures. This check does not enter the main estimate. Two
things to notice. First, the Swiss estimate is for a recurring annual tax. The paper argues that
taxpayers price the Act as the start of a recurring regime, so the recurring-tax estimate is the
right benchmark (PDF p.25). Second, the [BSZ report](../../bsz-analysis/site/) (Boll, Saez and
Zucman) disputes exactly this transfer ([disputes row 1](https://github.com/fhoces/opa-prop40/blob/main/comparison/DISPUTES.md)).

## Section 5.1: the income tax the billionaires pay

### The Pareto upper bound (eqs. 9 and 10)

$$N(y) = A\,y^{-\alpha}, \qquad S(k, n) = \left(\frac{k}{n}\right)^{(\alpha - 1)/\alpha}$$

The state publishes how many tax returns report income above \$1M, \$2M, \$3M, \$4M, \$5M and
\$10M (Franchise Tax Board, FTB below: Personal Income Tax Annual Report 2024, Table B-4A). If top incomes follow a Pareto distribution, the log
of those counts falls on a straight line against the log of the thresholds, with slope $-\alpha$.
The fitted line gives $\hat\alpha$ = **`r num(pf$alpha, 3)`** (printed `r out("pareto_alpha","printed_value")`,
$R^2$ = `r num(pf$r_squared, 4)`, PDF p.26).

```{r}
#| label: f-pareto
#| code-summary: "R code for the Pareto fit figure"
#| fig-cap: "The six published filer counts against their AGI thresholds, log-log, with the fitted Pareto line (paper Figure 1, PDF p.27)."
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 3.6
d <- data.frame(y = pf$thresholds, n = pf$filer_counts)
ggplot(d, aes(y, n)) +
  geom_abline(intercept = log10(pf$A), slope = -pf$alpha, linetype = 2, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_point(size = 2.5, colour = "#1f6fce") +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_dollar(scale = 1e-6, suffix = "M")) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(x = "AGI threshold", y = "Returns above the threshold") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```

$S(k, n)$ is the share of the bracket's income that goes to its top $k$ of $n$ filers. With the
top `r inp("n_billionaires")` of the 4,729 filers above \$10M, the continuous formula gives
`r pct(100 * sch$continuous_top_share)` of the bracket's \$`r inp("bracket_tax_ty23")`B of tax.
The script then builds a rank-by-rank income schedule and rescales it by
`r num(sch$rescale_factor, 3)` so that its top 212 match the continuous share (footnote 28,
PDF p.28: the discrete sum undershoots by about 11%). Scaling Tax Year 2023 to FY 2024-25 collections
(\$`r inp("total_pit_fy25")`B in total) multiplies by `r num(attr(itmc, "scale_factor"), 3)`. If
the billionaires *are* the 212 highest earners, they pay **\$`r num(t8$mean_fy25[t8$K == 212], 2)`B
a year**. That is the upper bound, and the top of $C$'s range.

### The dispersion Monte Carlo (Table 9)

Billionaires are ranked by wealth, not income, and many realise little income in a given year. So
the script places the 212 billionaires at random among the top $K$ filers (without replacement,
100,000 draws for each $K$ from 212 to 2,000) and sums their tax. The wider the pool, the lower the
expected total. The authors take $K \approx 500$ ("roughly the top decile of the bracket", PDF p.28)
as a reasonable floor, which gives the bottom of $C$'s range, \$3.3B. The choice of $K$ = 500 is a
judgement, not an estimate, so the range $C \in [3.3, 5.8]$ is labelled **guesswork** below.

```{r}
#| label: t-table8
#| results: asis
#| code-summary: "R code for Table 9"
p8 <- printed[printed$table == "table8", ]
pv <- function(k, col) p8$printed[p8$row == k & p8$column == col]
tab8 <- t8 %>% transmute(
  `Pool size K` = format(K, big.mark = ","),
  `Mean` = num(mean_fy25, 3), `printed` = sapply(K, pv, "mean"),
  `P5` = num(p05_fy25, 3), `printed ` = sapply(K, pv, "p05"),
  `P95` = num(p95_fy25, 3), `printed  ` = sapply(K, pv, "p95"))
m8 <- sum(round(t8$mean_fy25, 2) == sapply(t8$K, pv, "mean")) +
      sum(round(t8$p05_fy25, 2) == sapply(t8$K, pv, "p05")) +
      sum(round(t8$p95_fy25, 2) == sapply(t8$K, pv, "p95"))
scroll(kable(tab8, align = "rrrrrrr", caption = "Table 9, $B per year (PDF p.30)"))
```

`r m8` of the `r 3 * nrow(t8)` cells round to the printed value; the tests hold this at the printed rounding
(`tests/testthat/test-income-tax-mc.R`).

## Section 5.2: from an annual loss to a present value (eqs. 11 to 14)

$$PV = \frac{C}{r}, \qquad NPV = WT - f \cdot \frac{C}{r}$$

$$\text{or, with growth:}\qquad PV = \frac{C}{r - g}, \qquad NPV = WT - f \cdot \frac{C}{r - g}$$

This is the step that makes the result. The wealth tax is collected **once**. The income tax of
anyone who leaves is lost **every year, for ever**, and a perpetuity paying $C$ a year is worth
$C/r$ today. At $r$ = 1.5% a perpetuity is worth 1/0.015, about 67 years of payments; at 4.5%,
about 22. The paper's text then argues the lost stream grows with the billionaires' wealth, making
it a growing perpetuity, $C/(r-g)$ (PDF p.31). It calibrates $r - g$ at about 1.5% from the
S&P 500's dividend yield, and presents scenarios at 1.5%, 3.0% and 4.5% (PDF p.32).

Three things are worth knowing before reading the rest:

- **Which rate is drawn.** The Monte Carlo's eq. 18 and the code (`NPV_dist_v8.R`) call the 1.5% to
  4.5% draw $(r-g)$. The sentence after eq. 19 then computes $C/r$ (PDF p.35)
  ([mismatch 3](materials.html#mismatches)). Numerically nothing changes, because the same
  interval is used whatever it is called. Conceptually, the interval is asked to stand for two
  different things. The explorer's growth dial shows what the ambiguity is worth.
- **The loss is not scaled by $q$.** People who left do not come back if the Act is struck down,
  so the income tax loss stays even when the wealth tax collects nothing (PDF p.33).
- **The horizon.** Treating the loss as permanent is itself one of the disputed choices: the
  [BSZ report](../../bsz-analysis/site/) estimates the loss as lasting about the five payment years
  ([disputes row 2](https://github.com/fhoces/opa-prop40/blob/main/comparison/DISPUTES.md)).

## Section 5.3: the break-even departure share (Table 10, eq. 15)

$$x^* = \frac{WT \cdot (r - g)}{C}$$

Set NPV to zero and solve for the departure share: the tax pays for itself only if less than
$x^*$ of the income tax base leaves. The paper evaluates it at its central revenue,
\$`r num(0.5 * nb$wt_max, 0)`B ($q \times 72$), and the midpoint income tax, \$4.55B (PDF p.33).

```{r}
#| label: t-nber-table10
#| results: asis
#| code-summary: "R code for Table 10"
wt36 <- 0.5 * nb$wt_max
n10 <- compute_npv_table10(scenarios = list(central = list(label = "Central", WT = wt36, C = 4.55)))
pn <- printed[printed$table == "nber_table10", ]
mn10 <- sum(abs(round(100 * n10$break_even_pct, 1) - pn$printed[match(paste0("central@", n10$r), pn$row)]) < 1e-9)
scroll(kable(n10 %>% transmute(`WT ($B)` = num(WT, 0), `C ($B)` = num(C, 2), `r - g` = pct(100 * r),
                               `x*` = pct(100 * break_even_pct),
                               printed = pct(pn$printed[match(paste0("central@", r), pn$row)])),
             align = "rrrrr", caption = "Table 10 (PDF p.34)"))
```

`r mn10` of the `r nrow(n10)` cells match the printed digit. The central departure share,
$E[f]$ = `r num((nb$f_min + nb$f_max) / 2, 2)`, is above every one of them, which is why the mean
NPV comes out negative (PDF p.34). A check that is not an input: plugging each $x^*$ back into the
NPV formula must give exactly zero (see [internal identities](#internal-identities)).

## Section 5.4: the Monte Carlo behind the headline (eqs. 16 to 19) {#monte-carlo}

$$WT \sim U[\$0\text{B}, \$72\text{B}], \quad C \sim U[\$3.3\text{B}, \$5.8\text{B}], \quad
(r - g) \sim U[0.015, 0.045], \quad f \sim U[0.30, 0.60]$$

Draw the four inputs independently and uniformly, 100,000 times, and average the NPV
(PDF p.35). Two details matter:

1. **Revenue is drawn from zero.** The mean of $U[0, 72]$, \$`r num(h("nber","mc_expected_revenue"), 0)`B,
   is $0.5 \times 72$, the paper's central estimate (PDF p.33). This is the only place $q$
   appears in the code: there is no explicit multiplier ([mismatch 5](materials.html#mismatches)).
   A uniform draw from 0 is a different assumption from a survive-or-not coin flip on a fixed
   base. The two share a mean, not a distribution.
2. **The departure share is drawn on its own**, not tied to revenue. Revenue lost and income tax
   lost do not move together in a draw.

```{r}
#| label: t-mc
#| results: asis
#| code-summary: "R code for Section 5.4"
s <- tr("npv_mc_nber_summary")
scroll(kable(data.frame(
  ` ` = c("reproduced (seed 2026)", "printed (PDF p.35)"),
  `Mean` = c(num(s$mean, 2), num(h("nber", "mc_mean_npv", "printed"))),
  `Median` = c(num(s$median, 2), num(h("nber", "mc_median_npv", "printed"))),
  `SD` = c(num(s$sd, 2), num(h("nber", "mc_sd_npv", "printed"))),
  `% negative` = c(num(s$pct_negative, 2), num(h("nber", "mc_pct_negative", "printed"))),
  check.names = FALSE), align = "lrrrr",
  caption = "NPV Monte Carlo, $B, seed 2026, 100,000 draws"))
```

Our R port replays the authors' script exactly (same seed, same draw order) and agrees with an
unmodified run of `NPV_dist_v8.R` to machine precision (`tests/testthat/test-npv-mc.R`). The
printed summary reproduces to within Monte Carlo error, with no systematic gap. Its exact
expectation is `r num(tr("npv_mc_nber_analytic_mean"), 2)` \$B, which rounds to
`r num(tr("npv_mc_nber_analytic_mean"), 1)` rather than the printed
`r num(h("nber","mc_mean_npv","printed"))`: the printed value is the seeded run's, not the
expectation. The explorer shows the exact expectations and says so.

```{r}
#| label: f-npv
#| code-summary: "R code for the NPV distribution figure"
#| fig-cap: "The distribution of simulated NPV (paper Figure 3, PDF p.35). Draws below zero in orange; the dashed line is the mean."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.4
ggplot(data.frame(npv = mcn$draws$npv), aes(npv, fill = npv < 0)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, boundary = 0) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(mcn$draws$npv), linetype = 2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "#eb6834", `FALSE` = "#1f6fce"), guide = "none") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-250, 70)) +
  labs(x = "NPV, $B", y = "draws") + theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```

## Every input, by origin {#every-input-by-origin}

This section is not in the paper: it re-sorts every input by *how much evidence stands behind
it*, the question a reader who wants to argue with the result has to answer first.

- **data**: read off a public dataset or the authors' own person-level file, and recomputable from it.
- **research**: an estimate taken from a published paper.
- **guesswork**: set by assumption. Some are bounded by evidence, but no dataset or estimate pins
  the value itself.
- **scenario**: a choice about which policy or counterfactual is being estimated.
- **derived**: a value another row implies.

```{r}
#| label: origins
#| results: asis
#| code-summary: "R code for the input table"
dials <- site_dials(rc)
dial_rows <- do.call(rbind, lapply(dials, function(d) data.frame(
  input = d$key, what = d$label, `value(s)` = paste(d$labels, collapse = "; "),
  origin = d$origin, where = "explorer dial (R/site.R)", check.names = FALSE)))
# The rows only the first version uses (version "ssrn") go to the appendix.
first_only <- inputs$version == "ssrn"
inp_row <- function(x) data.frame(input = x$input_id, what = x$description,
  `value(s)` = ifelse(is.na(x$value), "1.5% to 4.5%", vapply(x$value, function(v) format(signif(v, 6)), "")),
  origin = x$label, where = x$source, check.names = FALSE)
odf <- rbind(inp_row(inputs[!first_only, ]), dial_rows)
scroll(kable(odf, caption = "Inputs by origin (export/r/inputs.csv, then the explorer's dials)"))
```

```{r}
#| label: origins-count
#| results: asis
#| code-summary: "R code for the input counts"
cnt <- as.data.frame(table(factor(odf$origin, levels = c("data", "research", "guesswork", "scenario", "derived"))))
names(cnt) <- c("origin", "rows")
n_guess_dials <- sum(vapply(dials, function(d) d$origin == "guesswork", logical(1)))
scroll(kable(cnt))
```

**The headline:** `r n_guess_dials` of the `r length(dials)` inputs that move the result in the
explorer are guesswork. The one labelled data, the revenue ceiling, rests on a legal judgement
about who counts as having left (disputes row 3). The data and research inputs (the Forbes base,
the FTB brackets, the Pareto fit) fix the *scale*; whether the NPV is negative is decided by the
guesswork: how wide the revenue draw is, where the income tax range stops, which rate is used, and
whether the lost income tax is permanent.^[The pipeline's input file also lists
`r sum(first_only)` rows sourced to the authors' first version (March 2026): its revenue floor,
its central scenario and the Swiss semi-elasticity as its workbook applies it. The
[appendix](#appendix-first-version) shows them.]

## What reproduces

```{r}
#| label: mismatch-summary
#| results: asis
#| code-summary: "R code for the output checks"
# The chapter's PDF page for each figure it prints (typed, like the printed values).
page_nber <- c(revenue_baseline = "19", nber_domestic_grown = "19", nber_ceiling = "21",
               nber_international = "17", pareto_alpha = "26", income_tax_mc_k212 = "30",
               income_tax_mc_k300 = "30", income_tax_mc_k500 = "30", npv_mc_nber_mean = "35",
               npv_mc_nber_median = "35", npv_mc_nber_pct_negative = "35")
ob <- outputs[outputs$output_id %in% names(page_nber), ]
o <- ob %>% transmute(output = output_id, reproduced = signif(value, 6),
  printed = printed_value, `abs diff` = signif(abs_diff, 2), page = page_nber[output_id])
scroll(kable(o, row.names = FALSE))
top_id <- ob$output_id[which.max(ob$abs_diff)]
stopifnot(top_id == "revenue_baseline")   # the prose below names it as mismatch 6
```

Every figure reproduces from the authors' own code to within the tolerances in
`tests/testthat/` (printed rounding for deterministic figures, four Monte Carlo standard errors
for simulated ones). The largest gap is `r top_id` (`r num(max(ob$abs_diff), 2)`), the baseline
of mismatch 6. Table 9's 21 cells and Table 10's 3 cells, shown above, match as well.^[The
first version's own outputs are in the [appendix](#appendix-first-version).]

```{r}
#| label: mismatch-list
#| results: asis
#| code-summary: "R code for the mismatch list"
mm_lines <- sub("^## ", "", grep("^## [0-9]+\\.", readLines("../MISMATCHES.md"), value = TRUE))
mm_first <- grepl("^[0-9]+\\. First version: ", mm_lines)
cat(length(mm_lines), " discrepancies were found between the authors' text, their READMEs and their code. ",
    sum(!mm_first), " of them concern the chapter. We record them rather than fix them:",
    "^[The other ", sum(mm_first), " concern only the authors' first version: ",
    paste(sub("First version: ", "", mm_lines[mm_first]), collapse = "; "), ".]\n\n", sep = "")
cat(paste0(mm_lines[!mm_first], collapse = "\n"), "\n\nFull text: [the materials page](materials.html#mismatches).\n")
```

### Internal identities {#internal-identities}

Checks against things that are not inputs to anything:

```{r}
#| label: identities
#| results: asis
#| code-summary: "R code for the consistency checks"
n_cell <- site_grid_cell(grid, as.list(site_named()$nber))
se_n <- mcn$summary$sd / sqrt(mcn$summary$n)
checks <- data.frame(
  identity = c(
    "Table 10's x* plugged into NPV = WT - x* C/r gives 0 (max |NPV|, $B)",
    "Grid's main-estimate cell equals the pipeline's analytic mean (abs diff, $B)",
    "Seeded MC mean vs exact expectation, in MC standard errors",
    "Share negative: quadrature vs seeded MC (points)",
    "Ceiling: domestic total minus the 7 departures, recomputed, minus the script's 72 ($B)"),
  value = c(max(abs(with(n10, WT - break_even_pct * C / r))),
    abs(n_cell$mean_npv - tr("npv_mc_nber_analytic_mean")),
    (mcn$summary$mean - tr("npv_mc_nber_analytic_mean")) / se_n,
    n_cell$pct_negative - mcn$summary$pct_negative,
    nc$ceiling_recomputed - nb$wt_max))
checks$value <- vapply(checks$value, function(v) format(signif(v, 3)), "")
scroll(kable(checks))
```

The seeded mean sits within about one Monte Carlo standard error of the exact expectation. The
printed `r num(h("nber","mc_mean_npv","printed"))` equals the rounded seeded run, not the rounded
expectation, `r num(tr("npv_mc_nber_analytic_mean"), 1)`. Which one a printed digit matches is a
rounding coincidence.^[In the authors' first version it is the other way round: its printed mean
equals the rounded expectation (see the [appendix](#appendix-first-version)).]

## Reproducing this document

```sh
cd rjkdc-analysis
export RAUH_REPO_DIR=/path/to/wealth_tax     # clone of github.com/bjaros20/wealth_tax at 25e84dd
Rscript -e 'targets::tar_make()'             # writes the targets store, export/r/, site/data/, site/explorer/grid.js
Rscript tests/testthat.R                     # full suite
quarto render site/repro.qmd
```

The authors' repository is MIT licensed but not redistributed here; the tests that re-run the
authors' own scripts skip cleanly without it, and the rest of the suite does not need it.

## Appendix: the authors' first version (March 2026) {#appendix-first-version}

This appendix is not part of the account above. It records what the pipeline also reproduces:
the authors' first version, Rauh, Jaros, Kearney, Doran and Cosso, *The Net Present Value of
the Billionaire Tax Act*, Hoover Institution, SSRN 6340778 (17 March 2026). Page numbers in this
appendix are that version's PDF pages. Its Pareto fit and income tax Monte Carlo are the ones in
Section 5.1 above (its Table 8 is the chapter's Table 9). Its revenue part and its Monte Carlo
differ.

**Revenue.** It starts from the same \$`r num(out("revenue_baseline","printed_value"), 2)`B baseline,
without growth to a valuation date or a litigation discount. Six confirmed departures leave
\$`r num(rc$confirmed6_ceiling, 2)`B (printed \$`r out("revenue_confirmed6","printed_value")`B,
p.11); ten reported departures leave \$`r num(rc$expanded10_estimate, 2)`B (printed
\$`r out("revenue_expanded10","printed_value")`B, p.13). The Swiss semi-elasticity, applied
linearly (10.32 × 5 = `r pct(100 * rc$migration_share)` of the base), gives
\$`r num(rc$literature_calibrated, 2)`B (printed \$`r out("revenue_literature_calibrated","printed_value")`B,
p.14). The preferred "approximately \$`r h("ssrn","revenue_headline","printed")` billion (range:
\$35-46 billion)" (p.14) is not computed anywhere in the authors' code. Every step after the
baseline uses a typed 94.2 rather than the workbook's 94.30 (mismatch 6).

**NPV by scenario and break-even (its Tables 9 and 10).** The departure share is tied to revenue,
$f = 1 - WT/94.2$, so revenue lost and income tax lost move together.

```{r}
#| label: t-table9
#| results: asis
#| code-summary: "R code for the first version's Table 9"
p9 <- printed[printed$table == "table9", ]
t9p <- t9 %>% mutate(key = paste0(scenario, "@", r)) %>% rowwise() %>% mutate(
  pv_printed = p9$printed[p9$row == key & p9$column == "pv_lost"],
  npv_printed = p9$printed[p9$row == key & p9$column == "npv"]) %>% ungroup()
tab9 <- t9p %>% transmute(Scenario = label, `WT ($B)` = num(WT, 2), `C ($B)` = num(C, 2),
  `f` = pct(100 * f), `r - g` = pct(100 * r),
  `PV lost` = num(pv_lost), `printed` = num(pv_printed),
  `NPV` = num(npv), `printed ` = num(npv_printed))
m9 <- sum(abs(round(t9p$pv_lost, 1) - t9p$pv_printed) < 1e-9) + sum(abs(round(t9p$npv, 1) - t9p$npv_printed) < 1e-9)
scroll(kable(tab9, align = "lrrrrrrrr", caption = "First version, Table 9, $B (its PDF p.19)"))
```

```{r}
#| label: t-table10
#| results: asis
#| code-summary: "R code for the first version's Table 10"
p10 <- printed[printed$table == "table10", ]
tab10 <- t10 %>% mutate(key = paste0(scenario, "@", r)) %>% rowwise() %>%
  mutate(printed = p10$printed[p10$row == key]) %>% ungroup() %>%
  transmute(Scenario = label, `r - g` = pct(100 * r), `x*` = pct(100 * break_even_pct),
            printed = pct(printed))
m10 <- sum(abs(round(100 * t10$break_even_pct, 1) -
  sapply(paste0(t10$scenario, "@", t10$r), function(k) p10$printed[p10$row == k])) < 1e-9)
scroll(kable(tab10, align = "lrrr", caption = "First version, Table 10 (its PDF p.20)"))
```

`r m9` of the `r 2 * nrow(t9p)` Table 9 cells and `r m10` of the `r nrow(t10)` Table 10 cells
match the printed digit. The central scenario's \$`r inp("wt_central_scenario")`B is a typed
literal with no derivation (mismatch 8). The headline is not a cell of Table 9: the central cell
at 1.5% is `r num(t9$npv[t9$scenario=="central" & t9$r==0.015])` \$B.

**Monte Carlo (its Sec 5.5).** It draws $WT \sim U[`r ss$wt_min`, `r ss$wt_max`]$,
$C \sim U[3.3, 5.8]$ and $r \sim U[0.015, 0.045]$, with $f = 1 - WT/94.2$. The paper prints the
upper bound as 67.1, a typo for 67.51 (mismatch 1). The text derives a growing perpetuity, but the
code divides by the plain rate (mismatch 2). The draw's revenue has a mean of
\$`r num(h("ssrn","mc_expected_revenue"), 2)`B, above the preferred
\$`r h("ssrn","revenue_headline","printed")`B.

```{r}
#| label: t-mc-first
#| results: asis
#| code-summary: "R code for the first version's Monte Carlo"
s1 <- tr("npv_mc_ssrn_summary")
scroll(kable(data.frame(
  ` ` = c("reproduced (seed 2026)", "printed (its PDF p.20)"),
  `Mean` = c(num(s1$mean, 2), num(h("ssrn", "mc_mean_npv", "printed"))),
  `Median` = c(num(s1$median, 2), num(h("ssrn", "mc_median_npv", "printed"))),
  `SD` = c(num(s1$sd, 2), num(h("ssrn", "mc_sd_npv", "printed"))),
  `% negative` = c(num(s1$pct_negative, 2), num(h("ssrn", "mc_pct_negative", "printed"))),
  check.names = FALSE), align = "lrrrr",
  caption = "First version, NPV Monte Carlo, $B, seed 2026, 100,000 draws"))
```

Our R port agrees with an unmodified run of `NPV_dist.R` to machine precision. The median and
share negative match the printed values. The mean (`r num(mcs$summary$mean, 2)` against
`r num(h("ssrn","mc_mean_npv","printed"))`) and the standard deviation
(`r num(mcs$summary$sd, 2)` against `r h("ssrn","mc_sd_npv","printed")`) do not quite
(mismatch 9). The draws are independent, so the mean has a closed form:

$$E[NPV] = E[WT] - \left(1 - \frac{E[WT]}{94.20}\right) E[C]\, E\!\left[\tfrac{1}{r}\right]$$

It equals **`r num(tr("npv_mc_ssrn_analytic_mean"), 3)` \$B**, which rounds to the printed
`r num(h("ssrn","mc_mean_npv","printed"))`. So the printed mean is the model's exact expectation,
while the shipped seed gives `r num(mcs$summary$mean, 2)`. The printed SD stays unexplained.

**Its outputs, inputs and checks.**

```{r}
#| label: first-version-tables
#| results: asis
#| code-summary: "R code for the first version's outputs, inputs and checks"
of <- outputs[!outputs$output_id %in% names(page_nber) & outputs$version != "nber", ]
scroll(kable(of %>% transmute(output = output_id, reproduced = signif(value, 6),
  printed = printed_value, `abs diff` = signif(abs_diff, 2), `its page` = printed_page),
  row.names = FALSE, caption = "First version: outputs"))
scroll(kable(inp_row(inputs[first_only, ]), row.names = FALSE, caption = "First version: inputs"))
x10 <- t10 %>% left_join(t9 %>% select(scenario, r, WT, C), by = c("scenario", "r", "WT", "C"))
s_cell <- site_grid_cell(grid, as.list(site_named()$ssrn))
se_s <- mcs$summary$sd / sqrt(mcs$summary$n)
checks1 <- data.frame(
  identity = c(
    "Table 10's x* plugged into Table 9's formula gives NPV = 0 (max |NPV|, $B)",
    "Grid's first-version cell equals the pipeline's analytic mean (abs diff, $B)",
    "Seeded MC mean vs exact expectation, in MC standard errors",
    "Share negative: quadrature vs seeded MC (points)"),
  value = c(max(abs(with(x10, WT - break_even_pct * C / r))),
    abs(s_cell$mean_npv - tr("npv_mc_ssrn_analytic_mean")),
    (mcs$summary$mean - tr("npv_mc_ssrn_analytic_mean")) / se_s,
    s_cell$pct_negative - mcs$summary$pct_negative))
checks1$value <- vapply(checks1$value, function(v) format(signif(v, 3)), "")
scroll(kable(checks1, caption = "First version: internal identities"))
```
